 Koenigsegg’s CC850 Recall Is a Software Story. For Collectors, That’s the Point
 Modern Car Collector Eve Nowell Thu, October 29, 2026 at 1:00 PM UTC Add to Preferred Sources Thu, October 29, 2026 at 1:00 PM UTC Koenigsegg’s CC850 Recall Is a Software Story. For Collectors, That’s the Point In the United States, the entire population of Koenigsegg CC850s could fit around a single dinner table. Seven cars, and as of October 21, seven entries in a federal filing. NHTSA Recall 26V694 covers every CC850 delivered to the American market, and the Koenigsegg CC850 recall it describes is narrow, specific and, by the manufacturer's own account, already corrected. That combination is exactly why it deserves a closer reading than the headline invites.
 What the filing actually says
 Koenigsegg's Part 573 report identifies a software condition in the electronic parking brake. With Reverse selected and the engine running, the brake does not stay engaged unless the driver holds the button down. If the car is left in that state, it can roll on a slope without any driver input. The affected cars were built between September 28, 2025 and August 2, 2026, and Koenigsegg estimates that 100 percent of them carry the condition.
 The trigger was a single field report on October 12: a driver left a CC850 on a slope with the engine running and Reverse engaged, and the car rolled. No injuries were reported. Koenigsegg opened an investigation that day, decided on October 19 to conduct a voluntary recall, and filed on October 21. The interim advice to owners is blunt: "Do Not Drive Park Outside."
 Advertisement Advertisement One detail deserves attention. The filing states that the condition does not constitute noncompliance with FMVSS 135 or UN R13-H, because it falls outside the static parking brake tests those standards prescribe. This was not a car that failed its homologation. It was a car that behaved in a way the test procedures never contemplated, which is a different and more modern kind of problem.
 Ten days, and no workshop
 Here is the part collectors should read twice. The remedy is a free over-the-air software update, scheduled to be available on October 22, ten days after the first report reached the factory. A dealer visit is the fallback only if an owner cannot complete the update remotely. The filing lists dealer and owner notification as October 26 in its form fields and October 29 in its schedule narrative; on either date, the fix was designed to reach the cars before the paper did.
 The filing also names the maker of the affected component as Koenigsegg Automotive AB itself. There is no supplier to chase, no parts allocation to wait on, no shipping container between the problem and the remedy. For an owner of a car this scarce, that vertical integration is the quiet reassurance inside a recall notice. It is also the reason the car is, in a meaningful sense, never finished.
 Seven cars out of seventy
 The CC850 is limited to 70 cars, according to Koenigsegg's own specification , which makes the American fleet one-tenth of the entire run. It is a deliberately engaged machine: a twin-turbo V8 producing 1,385 horsepower on E85 (1,185 on gasoline), a curb weight of 1,385 kilograms, and the Engage Shift System, which offers either a gated six-speed manual with a clutch pedal or a nine-speed automatic within the same transmission. It marks 20 years of Koenigsegg production and the 50th birthday of Christian von Koenigsegg, and it pays homage to the CC8S. The filing does not say which transmission the car that rolled was fitted with, and the defect is described entirely in terms of parking brake software, so we should not infer a connection.
 Advertisement Advertisement Nor should anyone infer much about values. Demand for cars like this is governed by allocation, specification and the maker's standing, and a software recall resolved within days is unlikely to disturb any of the three. Koenigsegg has weathered sharper scrutiny, including a public dispute over delivery delays and reliability , and has continued to deliver, most recently with the first Gemera customer cars following the Gemera's long road into production .
 What serious buyers should ask for
 The more useful question is what a recall does to a car's paper. A conventional collector car's build sheet closes the day it leaves the factory. The build sheet of a software-defined car never closes, because the car it describes keeps changing. It is a shift worth watching as the modern hypercar collector becomes a market force of its own, and it is why originality, for these cars, will increasingly mean a documented software history rather than an untouched one.
 In practice, a buyer of any recent Koenigsegg, or of any hypercar that receives updates from its maker, should expect a seller to produce the software version history, dated confirmation that open recalls were completed, and the manufacturer correspondence that accompanied them. A seller who can show an October 22 update logged against the VIN holds a stronger file than one who can only say it was probably done. The same discipline applies to cars with long competition lineages, such as the CCGT1 , where documentation is the difference between a story and a claim.
 The CC850 recall will be a footnote in the car's history, and it should be. But footnotes are what a provenance file is made of. Twenty years from now, the cars with a clean, dated, manufacturer-confirmed record of October 2026 will be the ones whose owners never had to explain it.
